why: A 70-restaurant pizza chain selling 1.4 million Margheritas a year (about 55 per restaurant a day) with mozzarella at $7 to $10 per kg and 0.2 kg per pizza is believable.

A council home-care charity with 6,300 clients, 248,000 visits a year (about 39 per client), £26 variable cost per visit and £3.2m fixed costs is believable, and the group shares and client counts add up with cost per client falling from Group A to E.
A $6.8 billion coatings maker eyeing a $62 billion national market within a $290 billion global one, with the top two provinces holding about half of it, is believable.
An online clothes retailer with about $1 billion a year in revenue and around $55 to $61 per order is believable, and the day counts and profit = revenue minus costs all check out.
A customs-duty recovery firm handling about 33,000 shipments a year with average declared values of 260,000, a 4% duty rate and the stated conversion rates is believable.
A national car park operator with 640 sites and about $940 million a year in revenue (about $1.5 million per site) is believable, and the half-year figures agree with the stated total.
Resort profits of $25-60 million offset by city hotel losses give totals that match the bar notes, and the margins imply steady sales of about $1 billion, which is believable for a hotel group.
Online profits of $50-70 million offset by shop losses give totals that match the bar notes, and the margins imply sales of $1.0-1.25 billion, which is believable for a book and stationery chain.
A 30-stall food hall surveying 5,000 visitors over a month is believable, and both pies add to 100%.
Year-on-year tourist arrival swings between -9.6% and +14.2% across four destinations are believable, and each highest growth figure is above its lowest.
